intro: Benno Moiseiwitsch plays “Clair de lune”, the third movement of Debussy’s Suite bergamasque. When the opening melody returns, it is an octave higher, and the moving piano figures of the middle section continue beneath it.

sections.label: A · Melody in paired notes
sections.mNote: Quiet thirds open into fuller, slower chords.

sections.label: B · Left-hand arpeggios under the theme
sections.mNote: The left hand plays arpeggios in D♭ major and C♯ minor.

sections.label: A′ · Opening melody an octave higher
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns over short arpeggios and held bass notes.

sections.label: Coda · Arpeggios descending to D♭ major
sections.mNote: High broken chords descend to the final D♭-major chord.

cues.title: Opening third, F and A♭
cues.text: The melody begins on F and A♭, a third played pp with no bass beneath it. The phrase moves in paired notes that separate and come together. Debussy marks it Andante très expressif, with the soft pedal down.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Suite bergamasque, III, bars 1–8: paired upper notes, pp and con sordina. Mutopia edition, transcribed from Fromont (1905). https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1778
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Verlaine’s poem, 1869
cues.text: In Verlaine’s Clair de lune, masked dancers play lutes under the moon. The poem describes them singing of love and good fortune while doubtful of their own happiness. It appeared in Fêtes galantes in 1869, and its first stanza names the bergamasques that also give Debussy’s suite its title.
cues.evidence: Paul Verlaine, Clair de lune, Fêtes galantes (1869), first and second stanzas. French text reproduced by the University of Chicago Press: https://press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/853446.html

cues.title: Un poco mosso, left-hand arpeggios
cues.text: D♭-major arpeggios spread out in the left hand beneath a new melody in longer notes. The marking is Un poco mosso, a little more movement.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), as transcribed in the Mutopia edition, bars 27–36: Un poco mosso, pp, D♭-major arpeggios beneath longer melody notes.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Middle section in C♯ minor
cues.text: The key signature changes from D♭ major to C♯ minor. Over a continuous rolling bass the melody rises, marked En animant, reaches forte at bar 41 and descends to Calmato at bar 43.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 37–43: C♯-minor signature, En animant, forte at bar 41 and Calmato at bar 43.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the opening melody
cues.text: At bar 51, marked Tempo I and ppp, the opening melody returns an octave higher. A low F sounds in the bass beneath it, and arpeggios open the bars under its paired notes.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 51–58: a Tempo I, ppp, opening melody an octave higher, F in the bass and arpeggiated accompaniment.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Moiseiwitsch recording, London, 1946
cues.text: Moiseiwitsch recorded Clair de lune at Abbey Road Studio 3 in London on 28 February 1946. His Master’s Voice issued the whole piece on one side of a 78 rpm disc, catalogue C.3485.
cues.evidence: Date, studio and matrix 2EA 10890-1: Moiseiwitsch chronology, entry BM-C#051, https://classical-pianists.net/viii/benno-moiseiwitsch/chronology-2/. Label, catalogue number C.3485 and one-side issue: https://archive.org/details/78_clair-de-lune-moonlight_benno-moiseiwitsch-debussy_gbia3042373b

cues.title: Ending in D♭ major
cues.text: Broken chords rise into the treble, then fall back towards D♭ major. Debussy marks the passage morendo jusqu’à la fin (dying away to the end). The final D♭-major chord is rolled across both hands and followed by a dotted-crotchet rest.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 66–72: morendo jusqu’à la fin, arpeggios and the final rolled D♭-major chord followed by a dotted-crotchet rest.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Held chords give way to arpeggios
transitions.to: B · Left-hand arpeggios under the theme
transitions.how: The piano’s high, held chords are marked dim. molto. At Un poco mosso, the left hand begins rolling D♭-major arpeggios, pianissimo, beneath a long upper note (bars 25–30 in the Fromont edition of 1905).
transitions.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 25–30: dim. molto, Un poco mosso and D♭-major arpeggios. The section begins within the held-chord preparation.

transitions.title: The opening tune returns over F
transitions.from: B · Left-hand arpeggios under the theme
transitions.to: A′ · Opening melody an octave higher
transitions.how: At Calmato the music returns to D♭ major after the C♯-minor climax. The left hand continues to move while the upper phrases grow softer. At a Tempo I the opening melody returns an octave higher over a low F, with short arpeggios beneath it, marked pianississimo.
transitions.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 43–58: Calmato, D♭-major signature and the a Tempo I return at bar 51.

transitions.title: Melody to closing arpeggios
transitions.from: A′ · Opening melody an octave higher
transitions.to: Coda · Arpeggios descending to D♭ major
transitions.how: The returning melody stops and broken chords climb into the treble over low D♭ and F in the bass. The whole passage is marked morendo jusqu’à la fin. After a last rise through D♭ major, both hands play a rolled chord, followed by a written rest.
transitions.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 65–72: final arpeggios, morendo jusqu’à la fin and D♭-major close.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
